# SK8022 — The assertion's expected and actual arguments are swapped

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An equality assertion is called as `(actual, expected)`: the `expected` argument is not a constant and the `actual` argument is, so the failure message names the two the wrong way round.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Tests |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S3415 |

## Why

The test passes and fails on exactly the same inputs; what is wrong is the diagnosis. `Assert.Equal(count, 3)` fails with "Expected: 0, Actual: 3" when `count` is 0 — which says the code produced 3 and the author wanted 0, the precise opposite of what happened. Every reading of that failure starts from a reversed diff, and the reader who trusts it goes looking for the bug in the wrong half of the program. The signal is one asymmetry and it needs no guess about intent: a constant cannot be produced by the code under test, so a constant in the `actual` position is the wrong way round.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Counts() {
    Assert.Equal(archetype.Count, 3);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Counts() {
    Assert.Equal(3, archetype.Count);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Evidence in one direction only.** The rule fires when the `expected` argument has no constant value and the `actual` argument has one. Both constant, or neither, is silence — there is nothing to distinguish the two and picking one would be a rewrite of somebody's test rather than a repair of it. ⚠ **xUnit, MSTest and NUnit, matched by parameter name rather than by a list of signatures.** The method must have exactly two parameters called `expected` and `actual`, in that order, on `Xunit.Assert`, `Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting.Assert`, `NUnit.Framework.Assert` or `NUnit.Framework.Legacy.ClassicAssert`. That is what covers `Equal`, `NotEqual`, `StrictEqual`, `Same`, `AreEqual`, `AreNotEqual` and `AreSame` without naming any of them, and it is also what excludes NUnit's constraint form — `Assert.That(actual, Is.EqualTo(expected))` is the opposite order and correct, and its parameters are not called this. A repository's own `Assert` class is not matched at all. ⚠ **Both parameters must have the same type, and that is what makes the fix safe rather than merely plausible.** Overload resolution and generic inference over two arguments of one parameter type are symmetric, so the reversed call binds to the same method with the same type arguments. Where the two types differ the reversed call can bind elsewhere or fail to infer — which is the failure docs/plan/08 records for `SK8002`, where `Assert.NotEqual(0, flags & Member)` does not compile because the `0` was an implicit constant conversion that the rewrite drops. ⚠ **A named argument is silence.** `Assert.Equal(actual: x, expected: 3)` states the order explicitly and is not wrong; swapping the positions would change what it means. ⚠ Reordering is unobservable as well as type-safe: the argument being moved is a constant, so it has no side effect and evaluation order cannot matter. ⚠ **A third argument stops the rule**, including a comparer or a precision, because the method then has three parameters and does not match.
